papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: Emergent Semantics Beyond Token Embeddings: Transformer LMs with Frozen Visual Unicode Representations
papers.research_question: Can semantic understanding in Transformer language models emerge without trainable, semantically-rich input embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs with frozen, non-semantic visual Unicode embeddings can learn semantic understanding and outperform identical models with trainable embeddings on reasoning benchmarks, indicating semantics are an emergent property of the architecture, not the input embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Semantics in neural language models is not a property of the embedding matrix but an emergent phenomenon of the model's layered composition and self-attention, opening new avenues for model standardization, modularity, and efficient scaling.
papers.key_findings:
Models with frozen visual Unicode embeddings converge, generate coherent text, and outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark.
Semantic clustering emerges in the deeper transformer layers, not in the input embeddings, as shown by t-SNE visualizations.
Even randomly initialized frozen embeddings allow the model to converge, suggesting semantic structures in trainable embeddings are an emergent artifact, not a prerequisite.
The 'representational interference' hypothesis posits that trainable embeddings are burdened with learning both structural and semantic features, leading to suboptimal performance.
Frozen embeddings provide a stable structural foundation, freeing the transformer's attention and feed-forward layers to focus on composing these primitives into high-level meaning.
papers.limitation:
The study was intentionally constrained in scale (0.3B parameters, 4B tokens); future work should test whether findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Generalization to truly novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures) remains an open question.
future_direction: Test whether these findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Explore the method's generalization to novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures).
Investigate applications in modular and standardized embeddings, efficient Mixture-of-Experts, and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.abstract: Understanding the locus of semantic representation in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for interpretability and architectural innovation. The dominant paradigm posits that trainable input embeddings serve as foundational "meaning vectors." This paper challenges that view. We construct Transformer models where the embedding layer is entirely frozen, with vectors derived not from data, but from the visual structure of Unicode glyphs. These non-semantic, precomputed visual embeddings are fixed throughout training. Our method is compatible with any tokenizer, including a novel Unicode-centric tokenizer we introduce to ensure universal text coverage. Despite the absence of trainable, semantically initialized embeddings, our models converge, generate coherent text, and, critically, outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark. We attribute this to "representational interference" in conventional models, where the embedding layer is burdened with learning both structural and semantic features. Our results indicate that high-level semantics are not inherent to input embeddings but are an emergent property of the Transformer's compositional architecture and data scale. This reframes the role of embeddings from meaning containers to structural primitives. We release all code and models to foster further research.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Tracing and Manipulating intermediate values in Neural Math Problem Solvers
papers.research_question: How are intermediate values of latent structured inputs (specifically arithmetic equations) encoded in a Transformer model's internal representations, and are these encoded features used during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that intermediate values in arithmetic problems are encoded in specific directions of a Transformer model's internal representations and that manipulating activations along these directions causally influences model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The case study shows how manipulations in activation space can find a causal connection to intermediate values, indicating that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, which is useful for enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals directions in the model's activation space that are highly correlated with intermediate values of arithmetic equations.
Manipulating model activations along these correlated directions changes the model's predictions in a way consistent with altering the corresponding intermediate value.
Not all directions with high correlation to an intermediate value are causally influential; some are correlated but do not determine model predictions.
The method combines tracing (correlation analysis) and manipulation (causal intervention) to establish a causal link between specific internal representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: How language models process complex input that requires multiple steps of inference is not well understood. Previous research has shown that information about intermediate values of these inputs can be extracted from the activations of the models, but it is unclear where that information is encoded and whether that information is indeed used during inference. We introduce a method for analyzing how a Transformer model processes these inputs by focusing on simple arithmetic problems and their intermediate values. To trace where information about intermediate values is encoded, we measure the correlation between intermediate values and the activations of the model using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, we perform a causal intervention by manipulating model weights. This intervention shows that the weights identified via tracing are not merely correlated with intermediate values, but causally related to model predictions. Our findings show that the model has a locality to certain intermediate values, and this is useful for enhancing the interpretability of the models.

papers.title: Neural Thermodynamics: Entropic Forces in Deep and Universal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do entropic forces arising from stochasticity and discrete-time updates in SGD govern representation learning and lead to emergent phenomena such as universal representation alignment and gradient balance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an entropic-force theory for SGD dynamics, showing that entropic forces break continuous parameter symmetries and lead to gradient balance phenomena and universal representation alignment.
papers.conclusion: Entropic forces and symmetry breaking unify various emergent phenomena in deep learning, such as progressive sharpening and universal representation alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Entropic forces break continuous parameter symmetries but preserve discrete ones.
Gradient balance (equipartition) emerges between layers and neurons due to entropic forces.
Entropic forces explain progressive sharpening and flattening of the loss landscape during training.
Entropic forces lead to universal representation alignment, providing a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Weight decay breaks the universal alignment, showing a trade-off between gradient balance and weight balance.
papers.limitation: The theory applies to SGD with small learning rates and weight decay; extensions to adaptive optimizers and large learning rates are future work.
future_direction: Extending the theory to adaptive optimizers and large learning rates.
Exploring the role of discrete symmetries.
Investigating the connection to biological learning.
papers.abstract: With the rapid discovery of emergent phenomena in deep learning and large language models, understanding their cause has become an urgent need. Here, we propose a rigorous entropic-force theory for understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. Building on the theory of parameter symmetries and an entropic loss landscape, we show that representation learning is crucially governed by emergent entropic forces arising from stochasticity and discrete-time updates. These forces systematically break continuous parameter symmetries and preserve discrete ones, leading to a series of gradient balance phenomena that resemble the equipartition property of thermal systems. These phenomena, in turn, (a) explain the universal alignment of neural representations between AI models and lead to a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, and (b) reconcile the seemingly contradictory observations of sharpness- and flatness-seeking behavior of deep learning optimization. Our theory and experiments demonstrate that a combination of entropic forces and symmetry breaking is key to understanding emergent phenomena in deep learning.

papers.title: A Neurocomputational Model of Grounded Language Comprehension and Production at the Sentence Level
papers.research_question: How can a neural network learn to comprehend and produce sentence-level language grounded in a virtual environment, and what internal representations does it learn?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation presents a neural network model that learns to map natural language questions to full-sentence answers using sublexical phoneme sequences, and introduces a novel training algorithm (LSTM-g) for second-order recurrent neural networks that uses only local computations.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation demonstrates that starting from a neural level can yield insights into cognitive representations and behaviors, and that the model provides a step towards more relatable and human-like language processing systems.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns combinatorial internal representations, enabling systematic generalization to novel sentences.
The model exhibits human-like critical period effects in second language acquisition when simulating memory development.
The LSTM-g training algorithm is effective and biologically plausible, requiring only local computations.
The model successfully grounds language in vision, learning to answer questions about a virtual environment.
The model learns via direct imitation of another speaker, emulating human language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The model uses a simplified virtual environment and a limited grammar, and does not handle complex sentences.
future_direction: Extend the model to more complex language and real-world perception.
Test the model on more psycholinguistic tasks to explore listener interpretations.
Investigate the emergence of syntax and other linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: While symbolic and statistical approaches to natural language processing have become undeniably impressive in recent years, such systems still display a tendency to make errors that are inscrutable to human onlookers. This disconnect with human processing may stem from the vast differences in the substrates that underly natural language processing in artificial systems versus biological systems. To create a more relatable system, this dissertation turns to the more biologically inspired substrate of neural networks, describing the design and implementation of a model that learns to comprehend and produce language at the sentence level. The model's task is to ground simulated speech streams, representing a simple subset of English, in terms of a virtual environment. The model learns to understand and answer full-sentence questions about the environment by mimicking the speech stream of another speaker, much as a human language learner would. It is the only known neural model to date that can learn to map natural language questions to full-sentence natural language answers, where both question and answer are represented sublexically as phoneme sequences. The model addresses important points for which most other models, neural and otherwise, fail to account. First, the model learns to ground its linguistic knowledge using human-like sensory representations, gaining language understanding at a deeper level than that of syntactic structure. Second, analysis provides evidence that the model learns combinatorial internal representations, thus gaining the compositionality of symbolic approaches to cognition, which is vital for computationally efficient encoding and decoding of meaning. The model does this while retaining the fully distributed representations characteristic of neural networks, providing the resistance to damage and graceful degradation that are generally lacking in symbolic and statistical approaches. Finally, the model learns via direct imitation of another speaker, allowing it to emulate human processing with greater fidelity, thus increasing the relatability of its behavior. Along the way, this dissertation develops a novel training algorithm that, for the first time, requires only local computations to train arbitrary second-order recurrent neural networks. This algorithm is evaluated on its overall efficacy, biological feasibility, and ability to reproduce peculiarities of human learning such as age-correlated effects in second language acquisition.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: TabPFN Through The Looking Glass: An interpretability study of TabPFN and its internal representations
papers.research_question: How does TabPFN, a tabular foundational model, process and transform input features? What information is encoded in its hidden representations and how do these representations evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that TabPFN encodes intermediate and final quantities of simple arithmetic tasks in its hidden representations in a linearly decodable manner, suggesting the model performs structured, hierarchical computation internally.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN implements systematic, hierarchical computation, with intermediate results linearly represented in the residual stream, moving towards more interpretable and trustworthy tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear regression coefficients can be linearly decoded from the model's hidden states within a single model fit, but not across different fits.
Intermediate arithmetic terms (e.g., a*b) are linearly decodable from middle-layer activations, indicating the model respects the order of operations.
The final answer can be decoded from hidden states earlier in the network (layer 5) than it is correctly projected to the output space via the logit lens (layer 8).
Input values and their linear combinations can be decoded from the activations of the answer token early in the model, suggesting a copying mechanism.
The model does not maintain a fixed, universal encoding of coefficients across different fits; representations are fit-specific.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple arithmetic (additive/multiplicative) toy expressions, unlike the highly complex, noisy functions found in real-world datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex, real-world functions.
Using mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching to find the mechanisms through which the answer is computed.
Manipulating the function through steering vectors or vector ablation.
papers.abstract: Tabular foundational models are pre-trained models designed for a wide range of tabular data tasks. They have shown strong performance across domains, yet their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. This lack of interpretability makes it important to study how these models process and transform input features. In this work, we analyze the information encoded inside the model's hidden representations and examine how these representations evolve across layers. We run a set of probing experiments that test for the presence of linear regression coefficients, intermediate values from complex expressions, and the final answer in early layers. These experiments allow us to reason about the computations the model performs internally. Our results provide evidence that meaningful and structured information is stored inside the representations of tabular foundational models. We observe clear signals that correspond to both intermediate and final quantities involved in the model's prediction process. This gives insight into how the model refines its inputs and how the final output emerges. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal mechanics of tabular foundational models. They show that these models encode concrete and interpretable information, which moves us closer to making their decision processes more transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: On the Binding Problem in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the underlying cause for neural networks' shortcoming in human-level generalization? The paper argues it is the binding problem, the inability to dynamically and flexibly bind distributed information.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a unifying framework for the binding problem in neural networks, organizing it into three aspects: segregation (forming entities from inputs), representation (maintaining separation of information), and composition (using entities for inference).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a compositional approach to AI, based on grounded symbol-like representations, is fundamental for human-level generalization, and hopes this survey serves as a reference and inspiration for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks lack the ability to dynamically bind distributed information, which is crucial for compositional understanding and systematic generalization.
The binding problem can be divided into three functional aspects: segregation, representation, and composition.
Solving the binding problem requires incorporating inductive biases that enable symbolic processing to emerge within connectionist frameworks.
Existing mechanisms like attention, memory, and graph neural networks partially address aspects of the binding problem but a unified solution is still needed.
A unified approach within connectionism is preferable to hybrid neuro-symbolic systems for achieving human-level generalization.
papers.abstract: Contemporary neural networks still fall short of human-level generalization, which extends far beyond our direct experiences. In this paper, we argue that the underlying cause for this shortcoming is their inability to dynamically and flexibly bind information that is distributed throughout the network. This binding problem affects their capacity to acquire a compositional understanding of the world in terms of symbol-like entities (like objects), which is crucial for generalizing in predictable and systematic ways. To address this issue, we propose a unifying framework that revolves around forming meaningful entities from unstructured sensory inputs (segregation), maintaining this separation of information at a representational level (representation), and using these entities to construct new inferences, predictions, and behaviors (composition). Our analysis draws inspiration from a wealth of research in neuroscience and cognitive psychology, and surveys relevant mechanisms from the machine learning literature, to help identify a combination of inductive biases that allow symbolic information processing to emerge naturally in neural networks. We believe that a compositional approach to AI, in terms of grounded symbol-like representations, is of fundamental importance for realizing human-level generalization, and we hope that this paper may contribute towards that goal as a reference and inspiration.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Biologically Plausible, Human‐Scale Knowledge Representation
papers.research_question: Can a neurally plausible model represent and manipulate structured knowledge at a human scale, specifically by encoding and decoding the main lexical relations in WordNet?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a biologically plausible spiking neural network that uses a Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA) to successfully encode and decode the structured knowledge in WordNet, demonstrating human-scale knowledge representation with plausible neural resource requirements.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that the presented approach is uniquely well-suited to providing a biologically plausible, human-scale account of the structured representations that underwrite cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The model achieved 100% accuracy in decoding individual WordNet concepts.
The model achieved 95.5% accuracy in traversing the WordNet hierarchy to arbitrary depth.
The model achieved 99.6% accuracy in decoding sentences constructed from WordNet concepts bound to roles.
The model uses about 2.5 million neurons, equivalent to approximately 14.7 mm² of cortex, which is biologically plausible and a significant improvement over prior approaches.
papers.abstract: Several approaches to implementing symbol-like representations in neurally plausible models have been proposed. These approaches include binding through synchrony (Shastri & Ajjanagadde, ), "mesh" binding (van der Velde & de Kamps, ), and conjunctive binding (Smolensky, ). Recent theoretical work has suggested that most of these methods will not scale well, that is, that they cannot encode structured representations using any of the tens of thousands of terms in the adult lexicon without making implausible resource assumptions. Here, we empirically demonstrate that the biologically plausible structured representations employed in the Semantic Pointer Architecture (SPA) approach to modeling cognition (Eliasmith, ) do scale appropriately. Specifically, we construct a spiking neural network of about 2.5 million neurons that employs semantic pointers to successfully encode and decode the main lexical relations in WordNet, which has over 100,000 terms. In addition, we show that the same representations can be employed to construct recursively structured sentences consisting of arbitrary WordNet concepts, while preserving the original lexical structure. We argue that these results suggest that semantic pointers are uniquely well-suited to providing a biologically plausible account of the structured representations that underwrite human cognition.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Transformer Dynamics: A neuroscientific approach to interpretability of large language models
papers.research_question: How does the residual stream in transformer models evolve across layers when viewed through a dynamical systems lens?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a dynamical systems framework for interpreting transformers, demonstrating that the residual stream exhibits continuous, accelerating, and rotational dynamics with attractor-like behavior in lower layers.
papers.conclusion: The dynamical systems approach provides a novel way to understand transformer computations, revealing low-dimensional dynamics and self-correcting properties that suggest stable computational channels.
papers.key_findings:
Individual units in the residual stream maintain strong correlations across layers despite the RS not being a privileged basis.
The residual stream accelerates and grows denser in activation magnitude as information progresses through the network's layers.
Mutual information between successive layers shows a sharp decline in early layers, coinciding with increasing linear correlations.
Individual residual stream units trace unstable periodic orbits in activation-gradient phase space.
Representations in the residual stream follow curved trajectories in reduced-dimensional space, exhibiting self-correcting, attractor-like dynamics in lower layers.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is based on a single model (Llama 3.1) and a specific dataset (WikiText), limiting generalizability.
The perturbation method ('teleporting' activations in reduced space) may not realistically capture how the model responds to more subtle changes.
The observed low-dimensional dynamics may reflect the simplicity of the language modeling task used; more complex tasks might reveal richer structures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other AI architectures with a residual stream, such as ResNets.
Investigate how whole sequences of tokens influence dynamics, not just the last token position.
Examine how the observed dynamics evolve over the course of model training.
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence models have exploded in scale and capability, understanding of their internal mechanisms remains a critical challenge. Inspired by the success of dynamical systems approaches in neuroscience, here we propose a novel framework for studying computations in deep learning systems. We focus on the residual stream (RS) in transformer models, conceptualizing it as a dynamical system evolving across layers. We find that activations of individual RS units exhibit strong continuity across layers, despite the RS being a non-privileged basis. Activations in the RS accelerate and grow denser over layers, while individual units trace unstable periodic orbits. In reduced-dimensional spaces, the RS follows a curved trajectory with attractor-like dynamics in the lower layers. These insights bridge dynamical systems theory and mechanistic interpretability, establishing a foundation for a "neuroscience of AI" that combines theoretical rigor with large-scale data analysis to advance our understanding of modern neural networks.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs: An Exploration Using Cognitive Dual-System Theory
papers.research_question: How can the contributions of knowledge retrieval and reasoning adjustment be separated and quantified in large language models during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cognition attribution framework based on dual-system theory to decouple knowledge and reasoning in LLMs, revealing domain-specific reasoning benefits, scaling effects, and a hierarchical separation of knowledge (lower layers) and reasoning (higher layers).
papers.conclusion: The proposed cognition attribution architecture offers a novel perspective for understanding LLM cognition and provides insights into scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and the reasoning limitations of small models.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, chemistry) and potentially impairing knowledge-intensive domains.
Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Scaling also makes reasoning significantly more prudent (reduces overthinking) and modestly more intelligent (increases correction) in specific domains.
Knowledge retrieval primarily occurs in lower network layers, while reasoning adjustments are localized in higher layers, suggesting a functional separation.
Small LLMs tend to overthink more than they correct during reasoning, leading to negative or limited reasoning gains.
LLMs exhibit a human-like anchoring effect, which reasoning adjustment helps to mitigate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA; future work should extend to open-ended generation.
The study does not include ultra-large models (>100B parameters).
The methods are simplified and may not fully capture the underlying mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to open-ended generation tasks.
Include ultra-large models (>100B parameters) in the study.
Conduct a more in-depth exploration of the phenomena observed using the framework.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) leverage both knowledge and reasoning during inference, the capacity to distinguish between them plays a pivotal role in model analysis, interpretability, and development. Inspired by dual-system cognitive theory, we propose a cognition attribution framework to decouple the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. In particular, the cognition of LLMs is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary phases: knowledge retrieval (Phase 1) and reasoning adjustment (Phase 2). To separate these phases, LLMs are prompted to generate answers under two different cognitive modes, fast thinking and slow thinking, respectively. The performance under different cognitive modes is analyzed to quantify the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. This architecture is employed to 15 LLMs across 3 datasets. Results reveal: (1) reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, and chemistry) and potentially imparing knowledge-intensive domains. (2) Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Additionally, parameter scaling make LLMs reasoning significantly more prudent, while moderately more intelligent. (3) Knowledge primarily resides in lower network layers, while reasoning operates in higher layers. Our framework not only helps understand LLMs from a "decoupling" perspective, but also provides new insights into existing research, including scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and limitations of small-model reasoning.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Understanding Empirical Unlearning with Combinatorial Interpretability
papers.research_question: Do unlearning methods truly remove knowledge of a target concept, or merely inhibit its expression while retaining the underlying information? How easily can supposedly erased knowledge be recovered through various fine-tuning operations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uses the combinatorial interpretability framework to show that unlearning methods do not fully remove knowledge; residual knowledge persists in model weights and can be recovered even when fine-tuning on unrelated data, with recovery tending to restore the original network encoding.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning methods leave residual knowledge that can be recovered, and recovery tends to reverse the erasure by moving weights back towards their original state.
papers.key_findings:
Supposedly erased knowledge persists in model weights in a way that can be detected with combinatorial interpretability.
This knowledge resurfaces when fine-tuning the erased model, even on non-target data.
Recovery occurs through a tendency to restore the original (pre-erasure) network encoding, as shown by a high parallel fraction in weight updates.
The encoding structure is largely preserved after Gradient Ascent and Task Vector erasure, but is substantially altered by Privacy Preserving Distillation.
Fine-tuning on unrelated data can recover erased concepts, suggesting erasure leaves residual knowledge attached to the edited weight structure.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on simple two-layer neural networks trained on synthetic DNF data, limiting direct applicability to larger, real-world models.
future_direction: Better understanding of when and why fine-tuning on non-target data restores the original encoding.
Assessing the applicability of these findings to larger models used in practice.
papers.abstract: While many recent methods aim to unlearn or remove knowledge from pretrained models, seemingly erased knowledge often persists and can be recovered in various ways. Because large foundation models are far from interpretable, understanding whether and how such knowledge persists remains a significant challenge. To address this, we turn to the recently developed framework of combinatorial interpretability. This framework, designed for two-layer neural networks, enables direct inspection of the knowledge encoded in the model weights. We reproduce baseline unlearning methods within the combinatorial interpretability setting and examine their behavior along two dimensions: (i) whether they truly remove knowledge of a target concept (the concept we wish to remove) or merely inhibit its expression while retaining the underlying information, and (ii) how easily the supposedly erased knowledge can be recovered through various fine-tuning operations. Our results shed light within a fully interpretable setting on how knowledge can persist despite unlearning and when it might resurface.

papers.title: Cognitive Activation and Chaotic Dynamics in Large Language Models: A Quasi-Lyapunov Analysis of Reasoning Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How can large language models with fixed parameters produce flexible and varied reasoning abilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the 'Cognitive Activation' theory and uses the Quasi-Lyapunov Exponent to show that LLM reasoning stems from a chaotic dynamic information extraction process in the parameter space.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit chaotic dynamics in their reasoning, and the Cognitive Activation theory provides a chaos theory framework for interpretability, revealing potential pathways for balancing creativity and reliability in model design.
papers.key_findings:
The model's information accumulation follows a nonlinear exponential law.
The MLP accounts for a higher proportion in the final output than the attention mechanism.
Minor initial value perturbations have a substantial impact on the model's reasoning ability, confirming LLMs are chaotic systems.
Deeper layers exhibit significant divergence in response to minor perturbations, while shallower layers are primarily convergent.
The final output is a linear sum of the outputs from all preceding MLP and attention modules, with the initial input becoming negligible.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of reasoning cognitive activation (e.g., chain-of-thought) presents additional complexities and will be addressed in future research.
Slight benign perturbations may trigger an 'avalanche effect', leading to broken reasoning chains or factual errors.
future_direction: Incorporate 'chaos control' mechanisms (e.g., dynamic regularization or attractor constraints) into model design.
Further validation of the hierarchical attractor pattern conjecture.
papers.abstract: The human-like reasoning capabilities exhibited by Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge the traditional neural network theory's understanding of the flexibility of fixed-parameter systems. This paper proposes the "Cognitive Activation" theory, revealing the essence of LLMs' reasoning mechanisms from the perspective of dynamic systems: the model's reasoning ability stems from a chaotic process of dynamic information extraction in the parameter space. By introducing the Quasi-Lyapunov Exponent (QLE), we quantitatively analyze the chaotic characteristics of the model at different layers. Experiments show that the model's information accumulation follows a nonlinear exponential law, and the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) accounts for a higher proportion in the final output than the attention mechanism. Further experiments indicate that minor initial value perturbations will have a substantial impact on the model's reasoning ability, confirming the theoretical analysis that large language models are chaotic systems. This research provides a chaos theory framework for the interpretability of LLMs' reasoning and reveals potential pathways for balancing creativity and reliability in model design.

papers.title: Text-Trained LLMs Can Zero-Shot Extrapolate PDE Dynamics, Revealing a Three-Stage In-Context Learning Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can text-trained LLMs zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and what is the in-context learning mechanism behind this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a three-stage progression from syntax imitation to exploratory high-entropy phase to confident prediction.
papers.conclusion: Text-trained LLMs exhibit emergent zero-shot capability to extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a consistent three-stage progression, revealing inductive biases analogous to numerical methods.
papers.key_findings:
One-step prediction accuracy improves with longer temporal context but degrades with finer spatial discretization.
Multi-step rollouts show algebraic error growth with time horizon, similar to classical numerical solvers.
Token-level entropy analysis reveals a three-stage ICL progression: syntax imitation, exploratory high-entropy phase, and confident prediction.
LLMs can sustain coherent multi-step rollouts for nonlinear PDEs like Allen-Cahn and wave equations.
The three-stage progression is consistent across model sizes and PDE types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities across a range of tasks, including zero-shot time-series forecasting. We show that text-trained foundation models can accurately extrapolate spatiotemporal dynamics from discretized partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without fine-tuning or natural language prompting. Predictive accuracy improves with longer temporal contexts but degrades at finer spatial discretizations. In multi-step rollouts, where the model recursively predicts future spatial states over multiple time steps, errors grow algebraically with the time horizon, reminiscent of global error accumulation in classical finite-difference solvers. We interpret these trends as in-context neural scaling laws, where prediction quality varies predictably with both context length and output length. To better understand how LLMs are able to internally process PDE solutions so as to accurately roll them out, we analyze token-level output distributions and uncover a consistent three-stage ICL progression: beginning with syntactic pattern imitation, transitioning through an exploratory high-entropy phase, and culminating in confident, numerically grounded predictions.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: EDUCE: Explaining model Decisions through Unsupervised Concepts Extraction
papers.research_question: How to build a self-interpretable model that provides explanations for predictions via unsupervised extraction of concepts from the input?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EDUCE, a self-interpretable model that predicts based on a binary concept representation and provides explanations via unsupervised extraction of semantically consistent concepts.
papers.conclusion: EDUCE is a self-interpretable model that extracts semantically meaningful concepts and grounds predictions on their presence/absence, generating relevant explanations while retaining high predictive performance.
papers.key_findings:
EDUCE achieves output accuracy comparable to baselines while providing interpretable concepts.
The concept loss improves concept consistency and separability compared to just sparsity constraints.
EDUCE extracts meaningful concepts that align with human intuition (e.g., politics, economy for news; positive/negative words for sentiment).
On multi-aspect sentiment analysis, some concepts correspond to specific aspects (e.g., appearance, smell).
The model also works on image data, extracting discriminative visual patterns.
papers.limitation:
There is a trade-off between interpretability and output accuracy, as the baseline model outperforms EDUCE.
On the multi-aspect sentiment analysis task, performance is lower than specialized models, and some extracted concepts may not align with gold rationales.
future_direction: Using hierarchical representations for concepts (e.g., WordNet).
Applying the principles to other input types (e.g., images).
papers.abstract: Providing explanations along with predictions is crucial in some text processing tasks. Therefore, we propose a new self-interpretable model that performs output prediction and simultaneously provides an explanation in terms of the presence of particular concepts in the input. To do so, our model's prediction relies solely on a low-dimensional binary representation of the input, where each feature denotes the presence or absence of concepts. The presence of a concept is decided from an excerpt i.e. a small sequence of consecutive words in the text. Relevant concepts for the prediction task at hand are automatically defined by our model, avoiding the need for concept-level annotations. To ease interpretability, we enforce that for each concept, the corresponding excerpts share similar semantics and are differentiable from each others. We experimentally demonstrate the relevance of our approach on text classification and multi-sentiment analysis tasks.

papers.title: Critical Phase Transition in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Are qualitative changes in Large Language Models, such as those induced by varying the temperature parameter, phase transitions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a phase transition occurs in practical LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, with critical behaviors similar to those in natural languages.
papers.conclusion: The extensive statistical analysis suggests that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, providing a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
A phase transition occurs at a critical temperature Tc ≈ 1, separating a low-temperature regime with repetitive structures from a high-temperature regime where generated sentences are often incomprehensible.
Near the critical point, sequences exhibit critical behaviors such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state.
Natural language datasets (OpenWebTextCorpus, WikiText) show critical properties similar to LLM-generated sequences at the transition temperature, suggesting LLMs are closest to natural language at criticality.
The low-temperature phase is ordered with chaotic repetitive structures (many peaks in power spectra), while the high-temperature phase is not simply disordered despite finite integrated correlation.
The phase transition is observed across different models (GPT-2, Japanese GPT-2, Pythia) and different mappings (POS tags, characters), indicating robustness.
papers.limitation:
The size of the models analyzed is moderate (70M, 124M, and 361M). Analysis of larger models is important because the true phase transition seems to exist in the large context window limit.
Further investigation is needed to better understand how the criticality relates to linguistic properties and practical tasks.
future_direction: Statistical analysis of larger models to confirm the phase transition in the large context window limit.
Precisely estimating the set of critical exponents for GPT-2, other LLMs, and multiple natural language corpora to classify the universality class.
Studying the potential phase transition at very low temperature between repetitive and deterministic phases.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance. To understand their behaviors, we need to consider the fact that LLMs sometimes show qualitative changes. The natural world also presents such changes called phase transitions, which are defined by singular, divergent statistical quantities. Therefore, an intriguing question is whether qualitative changes in LLMs are phase transitions. In this work, we have conducted extensive analysis on texts generated by LLMs and suggested that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter. Specifically, statistical quantities have divergent properties just at the point between the low-temperature regime, where LLMs generate sentences with clear repetitive structures, and the high-temperature regime, where generated sentences are often incomprehensible. In addition, critical behaviors near the phase transition point, such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state, are similar to those in natural languages. Our results suggest a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing.
